title: Hostages, Highway Blockades, and Three Dead Pastors: Manipur's Naga-Kuki Fault Line Has Cracked Open Again
excerpt: The killing of three Baptist church leaders on May 13 triggered a chain of retaliatory abductions across two districts. Thirteen civilians remain captive, and both the Naga and Kuki communities are now blockading highways and shutting down entire hill regions.
body:
The killing of three Baptist church leaders in Manipur's Kangpokpi district on May 13 has spiralled into the most dangerous escalation in the state's ethnic conflict since the large-scale violence of 2023. Thirteen civilians — six Naga and seven Kuki — remain in the hands of armed groups across two hill districts, and the community organisations on both sides have responded not with calls for restraint, but with shutdowns, highway blockades, and mass mobilisation.

This is not a new crisis. It is the latest and most volatile chapter in a conflict that has killed over 258 people, displaced 60,000, and destroyed hundreds of homes and religious sites since May 2023. But the hostage dimension — civilians held as bargaining chips across ethnic lines — has introduced a level of desperation that even by Manipur's grim standards feels qualitatively different.

## How It Unfolded

On May 13, suspected armed militants attacked a group of Baptist church leaders in Kangpokpi district, killing three and injuring four. The killings triggered a wave of retaliatory abductions across both Kangpokpi and neighbouring Senapati district. According to security officials, more than 40 people from both the Kuki and Naga communities were taken hostage by various armed groups in the hours and days that followed.

Through intensive negotiations involving state authorities, community leaders, and civil society organisations, 30 hostages were released on May 14 and 15. But 13 remain unaccounted for, and the rescue operations — involving joint combing by central and state security forces in the hill ranges northwest of Leilon Vaiphei and Kharam Vaiphei villages — have not yet located them.

## Two Communities, Two Shutdowns

The crisis has split Manipur's hill districts into two parallel zones of paralysis.

The Kuki Inpi Manipur, the apex Kuki community body, called a total shutdown across all Kuki-Zo inhabited areas beginning May 13 and has extended it repeatedly — most recently by another 48 hours from midnight on Sunday. KIM's information secretary, Janghaolun Haokip, cited the government's failure to respond to a charter of demands submitted to New Delhi on May 14 and the continued captivity of Kuki villagers in Senapati district. Thousands of Kuki-Zo protesters have rallied in Kangpokpi, demanding a National Investigation Agency probe into the church killings and the immediate release of all detainees.

On the Naga side, the United Naga Council has announced an inter-district economic blockade along national highways passing through Naga-inhabited areas — a tactic that, historically, has choked off essential supplies to large swathes of Manipur's hill population. The UNC's trigger is the abduction of six Naga civilians by suspected Kuki militants, a grievance that has hardened as days pass without their release.

Normal life across both Kuki-Zo and Naga hill areas has effectively ceased. Markets are shuttered, transport is halted, and the supply of food and fuel to remote villages — already precarious in the best of times — is under severe strain.

## The Deeper Fracture

What makes this crisis particularly alarming is that it involves not the Meitei-Kuki fault line that dominated the 2023 violence, but the Naga-Kuki divide — a secondary but increasingly volatile axis of tension in Manipur's complex ethnic mosaic. The Nagas and Kukis, both hill-dwelling communities with distinct tribal identities, have their own unresolved territorial and political disputes. The hostage crisis has collapsed any remaining space for dialogue between them.

The simultaneous mobilisation of the UNC and KIM — two powerful community organisations with the capacity to enforce blockades and shutdowns across vast hill territories — signals that the crisis has escalated beyond the capacity of local administration to manage. Both bodies are now making demands directly to the central government, and both have indicated they will not stand down until their people are returned.

## Why the Diaspora Is Watching

For the significant Manipuri diaspora — Meitei, Naga, and Kuki communities are spread across Delhi, Bengaluru, the UK, the US, and Southeast Asia — the cycle of violence at home is a source of deep anguish. Many diaspora members have family in the affected districts. Social media networks within these communities have been flooded with updates, pleas for information about missing relatives, and calls for international attention.

The diaspora's frustration is compounded by a sense that Manipur's crisis has been normalised — that the central government treats each new eruption as a local law-and-order problem rather than the structural failure it represents. The fact that tripartite talks between the Meitei, Kuki-Zo, and the Ministry of Home Affairs remain "inconclusive," as India Tribune reported, has reinforced that perception.

## What Resolution Looks Like

The immediate priority is the safe recovery of the 13 remaining hostages. Beyond that, the crisis demands what it has always demanded: a political process that addresses the underlying territorial and identity disputes driving the violence. The security forces can rescue hostages and enforce curfews, but they cannot resolve a conflict rooted in competing claims to land, autonomy, and recognition. Until that process begins in earnest, Manipur's hill districts will remain trapped in a cycle of violence, shutdowns, and despair.
